extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of Montaigne; readers of moral/philosophical essays
extracted.subtask_description: A Renaissance-style personal/moral essay that reflects on customs, virtue, and human conduct, using anecdote and classical authorities to advance normative observations. The page is Montaigne’s essay 'Of Cannibals', offering ethical criteria and evaluative judgments about culture, courage, and moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: “Callicles in Plato says, that the extremity of philosophy is hurtful, and advises not to dive into it beyond the limits of profit; that, taken moderately, it is pleasant and useful; but that in the end it renders a man brutish and vicious...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy should be pursued within practical bounds—pleasant and useful when moderate; excessive abstraction enslaves natural freedom and makes one contemptuous of religion, civil conversation, and human pleasures. Avoid extreme or impractical philosophical excess.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in conjugal affection
rubrics_metrics.description: “The love we bear to our wives is very lawful, and yet theology thinks fit to curb and restrain it... that the very pleasures we enjoy in the society of their wives are reproachable if immoderate, and that a licentious and riotous abuse of them is a fault as reprovable here as in illicit connections.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conjugal pleasures should be moderate, sober, and conscientious; immoderate sexual behaviour within marriage is morally reproachable and should be restrained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marriage as solemn/religious tie; sober delight
rubrics_metrics.description: “Marriage is a solemn and religious tie, and therefore the pleasure we extract from it should be a sober and serious delight, and mixed with a certain kind of gravity; it should be a sort of discreet and conscientious pleasure.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate marital conduct by seriousness and responsibility (generation and duty), not by wanton desire; pleasures appropriate to solemn institutions must show gravity and discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascetic remedies must be effective and proportionate
rubrics_metrics.description: Discussion of penances (watchings, fastings, hair-shirts, exile, imprisonment, whips) and the example of Gallio, whose prescribed penance became pleasure rather than cure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Penance and austerities used as remedies should be real, stinging, and effective; avoid artificial or performative austerities that fail their intended corrective purpose or merely become pleasures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward vulgar opinion; judge by reason and observation
rubrics_metrics.description: “How cautious men ought to be of taking things upon trust from vulgar opinion, and that we are to judge by the eye of reason, and not from common report.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct observation and reasoned judgment to rumor or popular belief; be cautious of accepting secondhand reports uncritically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer simple eyewitness testimony and write only what you know
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne prefers 'a plain ignorant fellow' as more likely to tell the truth because 'better-bred' men embellish; 'I would have every one write what he knows, and as much as he knows, but no more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value plain, firsthand testimony over polished but embellished accounts; authors should restrain themselves to their own knowledge and avoid extending claims beyond their experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethnocentrism when calling practices 'barbarous'
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is nothing barbarous and savage in this nation, by anything that I can gather, excepting, that every one gives the title of barbarism to everything that is not in use in his own country.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not label unfamiliar customs as barbarous simply because they differ from local practice; evaluate foreign customs by reasoned comparison, not mere difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value natural virtues over artificial refinements
rubrics_metrics.description: Passage arguing that in peoples less altered by artifice, 'the genuine, most useful, and natural virtues and properties are vigorous and sprightly' and that artifice has often degenerated natural qualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the worth of natural simplicity and virtues; do not automatically privilege cultural 'improvements' or artifices over natural goodness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barbarity is measured by cruelty and suffering, not novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: “I conceive there is more barbarity in eating a man alive, than when he is dead; in tearing a body limb from limb by racks and torments... than to roast and eat him after he is dead.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the moral gravity of practices by degree of inflicted suffering and cruelty rather than by how exotic or unfamiliar they appear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good teachers and moral authorities exhibit self-control
rubrics_metrics.description: “They are best taught who are best able to control and curb their own liberty;” (referring to divinity and philosophy's jurisdiction over private action).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral or religious instructors should demonstrate self-mastery; authority is supported by the instructor's personal restraint and example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability and dignity constrain permissible pleasures
rubrics_metrics.description: “All pleasures and all sorts of gratifications are not properly and fitly conferred upon all sorts of persons... All pleasures... are just and lawful, where intemperance and excess are not to be condemned.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a person's role, dignity, and context when judging which pleasures are fitting; moderation and appropriateness determine permissibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divination (extraordinary claims) demands accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: “Divination is a gift of God, and therefore to abuse it, ought to be a punishable imposture... Such as only meddle with things subject to the conduct of human capacity, are excusable... but those other fellows that come to delude us with assurances of an extraordinary faculty, beyond our understanding, ought they not to be punished, when they do not make good the effect of their promise?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extraordinary claims (prophecy, divination) should be held to account; fraudulent or failed claims deserve censure or punishment because they abuse public trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: True valour is courage of heart and will, not external trappings
rubrics_metrics.description: “The estimate and value of a man consist in the heart and in the will... Valour is stability, not of legs and arms, but of the courage and the soul... He that falls obstinate in his courage... he who, for any danger of imminent death, abates nothing of his assurance... is killed, not conquered.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate bravery by steadfastness and moral courage rather than by equipment, rank, or material advantages; heroic worth lies in inner constancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral measure of victory includes the conquered's moral admission
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation: 'Victoria nulla est, Quam quae confessor animo quoque subjugat hostes.' — 'No victory is complete, which the conquered do not admit to be so.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A victory's completeness includes the defeated acknowledging defeat in spirit; moral or psychological conquest matters, not only physical triumph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy and cheerful defiance under threat are honorable
rubrics_metrics.description: Description of prisoners who 'always appear with a cheerful countenance; importune their masters to make haste to bring them to the test, defy, rail at them...' and a song they sing inviting the enemy to 'dine upon him.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constancy, cheerfulness, and defiant dignity in the face of death are presented as marks of honor and should be admired when assessing character.
